segments.text: Welcome to a new week on Tesla Short's Time Daily Episode 526 for June 29th, 2026.
I'm Patrick, coming to you from Vancouver. Here's what's kicking off the week in Tesla land.
Texas regulators just cleared 84 Tesla Robo Taxis. The largest permitted autonomous fleet yet,
and the first real test of scaled FSD operations. Yesterday, we covered the latest on cyber
cab regulatory steps. Today, the story moves forward because the Texas state registry updated
its permitted autonomous fleet to 84 vehicles. Tesla plans to add cybercabs in Houston,
covering NRG Stadium, the airport, and Dijkian Park. That zone would give the company about 50%
more coverage area than Waymo currently operates in the city. The expansion positions Tesla for
scaled commercial operations ahead of the Q2 earnings report. State approval for the larger
fleet marks a clear regulatory step in one key market. Now, the software side is advancing across
the existing fleet. Build 2026.20.5.1 is rolling out FSD version 14 light to hardware 3 vehicles.
The update adds start self-driving from park, speed profiles, and arrival options to older cars.
This marks the first meaningful supervised update for hardware 3 in the version 14 series.
Tesla continues its effort to maintain software parity across the installed base.
Owners on hardware 3 are now seeing the same supervised feature set that newer cars received
earlier. The rollout began this week through the 2026.20.5.1 branch. While the software improves,
questions about accountability remain in the spotlight. Tesla's head of AI confirmed that
the June 19 fatal Model 3 crash in Texas followed a full accelerator override by the driver.
Vehicle logs showed the accelerator input reached 100% and held at 73 miles per hour through
impact. The data also showed FSD was already disengaged before the collision. Fleet telemetry
therefore served both to train the system and to resolve the public record of the event.
This dual use of vehicle data turns every Tesla into a rolling sensor array that records exactly
what happened in the moments before any incident. When regulators or media question whether autonomy
software caused the crash, the same logs that enable continuous improvement also serve as the
definitive record of driver intervention. This dual use means Tesla can resolve disputes faster
than competitors who lack equivalent telemetry, yet it also raises the bar for what counts as proof
in public debate. The recent Texas crash illustrates the point. Vehicle data showed the driver
pressed the accelerator to 100%, overriding the system and sustaining that input through impact.
Without that granular trace, speculation would have continued for weeks. Over time, this capability
changes the economics of liability. Insurers and courts gain access to objective sequences
rather than reconstructions, which should compress settlement cycles and reduce uncertainty.
The open question is whether the public and regulators will consistently accept the data as
authoritative when the outcome is unfavorable to Tesla. Tesla published a detailed guide addressing
frequent misconceptions about charging speed, battery health, and infrastructure limits. The material
draws on fleet data to correct common assumptions about how quickly batteries can accept power under
varying conditions. It also covers how repeated fast charging sessions affect long-term capacity
retention across different climates and usage patterns. The explainer walks through real world
limits on station throughput when multiple vehicles arrive at once. Tesla used aggregated logs
from thousands of vehicles to show typical charge curves rather than peak lab numbers.
Owners can now reference the document when comparing station performance against marketing claims
from other networks. A new patent describes an autoregressive transformer approach that tokenizes
intersections to improve lane connectivity decisions. The method treats complex junctions as
sequence prediction problems instead of isolated rule checks. It breaks down each intersection into
ordered tokens that represent possible lane paths and their connections. Training draws on fleet
video to predict the most likely next lane state after the current one. The approach aims to reduce
incorrect lane selections at multi-leg or offset intersections where traditional mapping falls short.
Tesla filed the work as a way to handle edge cases that current supervised stacks still encounter
during urban drives. Industry forecast for Q2 show GM, Ford, and Tesla projected to lose US
market share. The shift reflects changing competitive dynamics in the domestic market as other brands
gain ground. Tesla's portion of the overall vehicle mix is expected to decline alongside the two
legacy automakers. The projections factor in rising inventory levels at non-Tesla dealerships
and expanded model availability from newer entrants. All three companies face pressure from both
traditional rivals and newer EV focus brands in the same period. The data covers light vehicle
registrations across the full quarter ending in June. Ross Gerber called for Tesla to prioritize
vehicle sales and margins after recent stock weakness. The comments highlight ongoing tension between
autonomy ambitions and near-term product execution. Gerber urged management to refocus resources on
the core automotive business rather than spreading efforts across multiple future programs.
The statement came as part of a broader investor note that questioned whether current valuation
levels match delivery trends. Tesla has not issued a direct response to the specific recommendations
in the note. A head-to-head test pits the Model Y against the Zekers 7X, Cooper Terramar, Toyota
RAV4, and Mazda CX-5 for 2026 medium SUV honors. The evaluation covers ride quality over varied road
surfaces and real-world efficiency measured on identical routes. Testors also measured interior
cargo space with rear seats in both upright and folded positions. The Zekers 7X posted competitive
acceleration and tech features while the RAV4 emphasized reliability data from prior model years.
Model Y scored highest in the group for software update frequency and over-the-air feature additions.
The comparison used production vehicles purchased through normal retail channels rather than
press fleet units. Owners continue to highlight the seamless integration of software and hardware as
the core reason daily driving feels smoother than in other vehicles. The discussion centers on how
over-the-air updates accumulate small handling and interface changes across months rather than
delivering one dramatic new feature. Drivers note that the same car behaves differently after
several updates without any hardware swap. The effect appears most noticeable in stop-and-go traffic
and highway lane changes where the system anticipates driver preferences. No single release
accounts for the overall impression reported across multiple owner threads. A recent clip shows
supervised FSD making an unexpected maneuver at an intersection, prompting discussion about
sign relevance and edge case handling. The low-resolution footage limits detailed analysis but sparked
debate on whether certain stop sign rules are outdated for current traffic patterns.
Viewers questioned whether the system correctly waited a faded sign versus surrounding
vehicle behavior. The incident occurred on a residential street with partial tree cover affecting
camera clarity. No injuries or property damage were reported in the clip. Now shifting to the
competitive picture in Europe. BYD has overtaken Tesla in recent European EV registrations. The Chinese
brand moved ahead on lower prices and a wider model range. Tesla's share declined amid
shifting buyer sentiment and expanded Chinese dealer networks. The gap reflects both price
competition and external sentiment factors in the region. Tesla will need stronger product
refreshes or pricing responses to regain ground. This near-term pressure in a key market stands
in contrast to the regulatory progress seen in Texas. On the customer side, Tesla launched a contest
offering lifetime free supercharging. Nine drivers will receive the prize based on the highest
number of charging sessions completed. The program aims to increase utilization at existing
stations. Higher session volume helps spread fixed station costs across more users.
The contest runs as a direct engagement play to drive more activity on the current network.
Meanwhile, Tesla and SpaceX are expanding their technology collaboration.
Reports point to deeper work on shared battery and autonomy components. Tesla shares moved
higher following the news of the expanded partnership. The collaboration builds on existing work
in supply chain areas that both companies already share. This supply chain angle adds another layer
to Tesla's broader technology bets beyond the vehicle business itself. Before we go, keep an eye
on further details around the Houston Robotaxi zones and any fresh regulatory updates expected
after the earnings report. That's your Tesla news for today. TSLA closed at $379.71
up $4.59 1.2%. If you found this useful, a rating or review on Apple podcasts or Spotify
